newsitem.title: UK: Markets on U.S interest rate alert next week.
newsitem.headline: Markets on U.S interest rate alert next week.

text.p: Financial markets will scour key U.S. price data in the coming week, eager for clues on the timing of the next U.S. rate rise, economists said on Friday.
But a wealth of British data, a possible firm date for the British election and the German Ifo survey and M3 figures, will provide plenty of domestic fodder for European markets too.
"Markets remain on interest rate alert," said Nick Stamenkovic, international economist at DKB International here.

"We've got key U.S. CPI figures on Wednesday, and in view of (last) Thursday's strong retail sales data...if we see any sign of inflationary pressures, then that will increase the risk of the Fed moving at the March FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee)."
U.S. February consumer price data, due 1330 GMT on Wednesday, are expected to show a modest monthly rise.
"We expect it to be bond market friendly, but any bad news will increase the chances of a rate hike," Stamenkovic added.
The U.S. Federal Open Market Committee is due to meet on March 25.
Economists are divided over the chances of an interest rate rise, but agree the coming week's figures will help shape expectations.
"The CPI data are hugely important because any indication of an acceleration there will be seen as increasing the likelihood of a rate hike," said Bank America senior economic adviser Jeremy Hawkins.
He said he expected the CPI to be moderate, but added U.S. housing starts, due on Tuesday, would show a bounce.
"There's an ongoing dichotomy between the real side numbers and the inflation figures in the U.S.," said Hawkins.
"It's a case of whether the Fed will tighten pre-emptively or wait for the inflation numbers to deteriorate first."
Markets will glean further clues on the Fed's intentions on Thursday when Greenspan testifies to the joint economic committe on Fed policy.

"We expect him to reiterate his message from the Humphrey Hawkins testimony, and suggest risks to inflation remain on the upside," said Stamenkovic. "The Fed are prepared to raise rates but they need something to hang that on."

While European debt markets will be dictated largely by U.S. interest rate sentiment, events closer to home will also garner some attention, economists said. "Germany's Ifo survey could underpin Bunds and be negative for Spain and Italy," said Phyllis Reed, European bond strategist at BZW.
"If the numbers are even marginally weaker than expected, it will open up the question of whether the single currency can go ahead." The IFO report is expected to be released on Thursday.
A wealth of data from Britain combined with growing speculation that Prime Minister John Major is on the verge of naming the election day will also keep gilts on their toes.
"The initial reaction (to the election date) will be interesting," said Reed. "If the (gilt) market doesn't go down, you could see a number of investors looking to buy."
UK January average earnings and unit wage costs plus February unemployment and retail sales data are due on Wednesday, followed by February retail price data on Thursday.

"Next week's data should reinforce the Chancellor's hand," said Stamenkovic. "Wage pressure will remain subdued and inflation data should show the chances of the government hitting its inflation target by early summer increasing."
